analysis.one_liner: Restores Commodity Futures Trading Commission oversight of energy derivatives traded on electronic platforms.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with no cosponsors, was sent to a House Agriculture subcommittee and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would close a regulatory loophole in energy trading. Under current law, large companies can trade energy derivative contracts with each other on private electronic trading systems without any oversight by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal agency that watches futures markets. The bill would repeal that exemption for energy derivatives, putting those transactions back under the agency's jurisdiction.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary energy consumers and the integrity of energy markets generally. The bill would give the CFTC authority to oversee wholesale energy derivative trading that currently happens off the books, which is the kind of unregulated trading that can distort the prices households and businesses ultimately pay for electricity and natural gas.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the exemption that lets energy derivative contracts traded between large commercial entities on electronic trading facilities escape Commodity Futures Trading Commission oversight, placing those transactions fully under the agency's jurisdiction. [S2]

It does this by striking the relevant paragraphs of the Commodity Exchange Act's electronic trading exemption, while keeping the separate 1993 exemption for energy products, narrowing the change to the electronic trading gap. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Companies that trade energy derivatives on private electronic platforms — typically large energy merchants and their trading arms — would face federal oversight, reporting, and anti-manipulation rules for trades that are currently unregulated.

drawbacks.text: Traders of exempt commercial energy contracts have long argued that regulatory oversight adds compliance costs and could push some trading to overseas or other unregulated venues; the bill would impose those costs on firms trading energy derivatives electronically between themselves. [S2]

The bill restores oversight only for electronic trading of energy derivatives between eligible commercial entities; it explicitly maintains the 1993 energy products exemption for other bilateral energy trades, so much wholesale energy derivative activity would remain outside CFTC jurisdiction. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit — bringing wholesale energy derivative trading on electronic platforms back under a federal anti-manipulation watchdog — is broad but indirect, reaching consumers through healthier energy markets rather than through direct payments. The cost falls on a narrow group of large trading firms in the form of compliance and oversight. The bill's main design weakness is that it leaves other energy derivative exemptions intact, so it is a partial fix rather than a comprehensive one.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Agriculture Committee and then to a subcommittee, and it stayed there until the Congress ended without ever getting a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

narrative.text: Representative Carolyn Maloney, a New York Democrat, introduced the bill on March 7, 2002, with no cosponsors. [S4]

The House referred it to the Agriculture Committee on the day it was introduced — the committee that handles commodities law — and a week later sent it to the Subcommittee on Farm Commodities and Risk Management. [S5]
No further action appears in the record; the bill died at the end of the 107th Congress in January 2003 without a vote in the House. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firms that trade energy derivatives on private electronic platforms are better off, since the loophole the bill would have closed stays open and those trades remain outside CFTC oversight.

for.name: Carolyn Maloney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restore CFTC oversight of electronic energy derivatives trading.

against.name: Larry Combest
against.what_they_did: The Agriculture Committee, which he chaired, never scheduled a markup or hearing on the bill, and it died in committee without a vote.

against.name: Subcommittee on Farm Commodities and Risk Management
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 14, 2002 and took no action on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors, so there is no record of how members of either party would have lined up.

industries.industry: Energy derivatives traders and electronic energy trading platforms
industries.note: The bill would subject their currently exempt trades to CFTC oversight, including anti-manipulation rules. The exemption lets large firms trade energy derivatives among themselves without a federal regulator, and the price distortions that can result ultimately reach ordinary households through energy bills.

The bill maintains the 1993 energy products exemption and targets only electronic principal-to-principal trading, so established regulated exchanges do not lose ground and may benefit if oversight shifts activity their way. [S3]
The bill restores the agency's jurisdiction over energy derivatives traded on electronic facilities, expanding the markets it can police. [S2]
